edges.effect_quant: Observational syntheses often suggest lower gastric-cancer risk with long-term or higher-dose green-tea intake, but the cohort evidence is weaker and sometimes null.
edges.mechanism: Green tea may influence gastric carcinogenesis through antioxidant activity, antimicrobial effects relevant to Helicobacter pylori, and modulation of mucosal inflammation. Temperature of intake and regional preparation habits matter here, which means the exposure can be partly protective in one setting and partly harmful in another.
edges.summary: The literature points in a generally favorable direction, but not cleanly enough to treat this as a settled prevention edge. Case-control and dose-response analyses often show lower gastric-cancer risk with long-term green-tea intake, while cohort-focused analyses are softer, so the best label is mixed evidence with a possible protective signal.
edges.caveats: Several studies combine green tea with other tea patterns, and very hot tea may independently raise upper-GI cancer risk. Geography and Helicobacter pylori prevalence also complicate how transportable any pooled estimate really is.
